summary: 1. Replace title questions with a bold sensory contrast or counter-intuitive claim in the first sentence instead of repeating the title. 2. Anchor hooks to hyper-relatable physical metaphors (e.g., '3 cars on your teeth') rather than abstract facts. 3. Write titles in conversational Devanagari-Hinglish paired with an emoji rather than formal academic Hindi or pure English. 4. Focus topics on visceral pop-science (predator mechanics, crash survival) over industrial engineering or niche chemistry. 5. Target sub-40-second pacing; high-retention shorts drop retention steeply when bloated past 45 seconds.
winning_hooks: सोचो, तुम्हारे दांतों पर 3 छोटी cars एक के ऊपर एक रख दी जाएं। इतने ज़ोर से T. rex काटता था। (Visceral second-person sensory anchor)
Movies में T. rex गाड़ी का पीछा करता है। पर असली T. rex शायद दौड़ ही नहीं सकता था। (Immediate pop-culture myth debunk)
जो car crash में पिचक जाती है, वो तुम्हें ज़्यादा बचाती है। (Counter-intuitive absolute claim in under 10 words)
avoid: Never repeat the exact title wording in the first spoken line (e.g., repeating the 250 km/h hydroplaning question tanked stayed rate to 30.6%).
Never use passive textbook phrasing or documentary-style introductions (e.g., 'Kuch everyday objects mein secretly...').
Never use academic, formal Hindi text walls in titles (e.g., 'जीवाश्मों में मिली रहस्यमयी आकृतियां...').
Never publish purely English titles on this channel (produced the worst drop-off at 6.7% stayed).
next_experiment: A/B test Hook Structure on the same topic: Script A opens with a counter-intuitive assertion ('तुम्हारी कार का शीशा तुम्हें बचाने के लिए जानबूझकर तोड़ा जाता है'), Script B opens with a second-person sensory scenario ('सोचो अगर 100 की speed पर कार का शीशा चेहरे पर टूट पड़े'), holding title, length (under 35s), and thumbnail constant.
